messages.body_plain:
Hi Christy,
It sounds to me like you could use the standard occupancy model (single species, single season -- function occu() in unmarked) to proceed. You would have 30 sites, each with 6 total surveys (one traditional and molecular survey for each of 3 occasions). You can use a binary survey-level covariate to differentiate the traditional surveys from the molecular surveys, and can use AICc to see if there is support for a method-level effect on detection.

You might also look into the "multi-method" or "multi-scale" model by Nichols et al. (2008). This model would be preferred if you thought the occupancy state changed from occasion 1 to 2 to 3, so depending on the temporal scale of sampling you may or may not be interested in this. While this model isn't implemented in unmarked yet, it can be implemented in MARK and Presence. It can also be implemented in R via package eDNAoccupancy (Dorazio and Erickson, 2017). Ideally you'd have some additional survey replicates at each occasion, but I wanted to mention it in case it becomes useful to you in the future. The eDNA/aquatic detection field seems to be embracing this model for data similar to yours.

Dorazio, Robert M., and Richard A. Erickson. "ednaoccupancy: An r package for multiscale occupancy modelling of environmental DNA data." Molecular ecology resources (2017).

Nichols, James D., et al. "Multi‐scale occupancy estimation and modelling using multiple detection methods." Journal of Applied Ecology 45.5 (2008): 1321-1329.

Best,
Brittany

messages.body_plain:
Dear people who are much smarter than me,

I have had great success using unmarked to run dynamic occupancy models (colext) for Blue-spotted Salamanders (first chapter of dissertation).

I'm now interested in community level effects of management. I am working through Chapter 11 of the AHM book. For data, I have:

Presence/absence data for birds (point counts), mammals (cameras and Sherman trapping), and herps (cover boards, hoop nets) for 232 randomly distributed plots across 55 forest preserves.
he monitoring program has been running for 8 years so far, but due to logistics, all the sites were not sampled each year.
Across these preserves, 159 have been surveyed every other year (so at least 4 seasons of presence/absence) and 74 have been surveyed every 4 years (so 2 seasons).
In addition, each site has multiple surveys per year when surveyed (ie, 2+ point counts, 4 days of turtle trapping, 4 days of camera trapping, etc.
I also have really nice information on management: 1500 events of chemical management for invasive species, 471 events of mechanical management (mowing, etc.), and data on 2105 prescribed burns.

I'd like to use more modern methods of community analysis, i.e. those that incorporate imperfect detectability for my third and final dissertation chapter.

And now my question(s):

Is this possible without delving into the realm of Bayesian methods? While I see the utility and value of learning and applying the models of Dorazio et al. 2010, Kery and Royle 2016, or one of the Zipkin models, I do not think I have the stats background to do so effectively or responsibly. My university (I'm a PhD student working on wildlife conservation in small general "biological sciences" department) doesn't offer a course Bayesian modeling, and it was hard enough for me to wrap my head around the dynamic occupancy models.

That said, I was reading in Conroy and Carrol (2009; Quantitative Conservation of Vertebrates) that one could use single-season occupancy models to estimate communties. Is it possible (or more rather, reasonable) to extend that technique and apply it to multi-season occupancy models?

Sorry if this was a big build-up for a rather small question!

I'd also be interested in any online courses that cover applied bayesian modelling, rather than workshops (new infant at home!), so if there are any of those you'd recommend, I could probably get my university or grant agency to cover it.

Thanks in advance,
John

PS: any plans on incorporating species co-existence occupancy models into unmarked? I'll be using these for my 2nd chapter.

messages.body_plain:
Hey John,

I'd be interested to hear what others think, but real quick: there's a longer history of "stacking" independent single species models for community analysis than explicitly incorporating multiple species within an analysis. The advantages of the multi-species approach are a) treating species as "random effects" will help pull parameter estimates associated with really sparsely observed species into line, b) you might be explicitly interested in covariance between species occurring, persisting, colonizing etc., and c) there's some opportunity to explicitly test things like whether richness varies across some space/time gradient rather than use correlation after the fact (Chris Sutherland, Simone Tenan, and others have 1 or 2 papers on this that specifically focus on spatial variability, [I think?], but you could stack preserve x time and treat them as separate preserves). As far as evaluating the mean response to management action x or interspecific variability in response to action x,  I'd argue that treating species independently is probably okay if you think of this as something like a meta-analysis and analyze it that way.

Cheers,

John

hi Laura,
 the model implemented in distsamp is a SITE-level model, using site level totals (per distance class) and therefore it requires site level covariate summaries. Thus if you have within-site covariates you must aggregate them up to the level of the site.
 It is possible to model within-site covariates (e.g., see chapter 9 of the AHM book), and we have a hacked function in unmarked called pcount.spHDS for that, but it requires a complete raster coverage of the covariate (not sampled)
 Also see this really great paper here

Hello all,

Is there a problem with using the same covariate (or highly correlated covariates) in both psi and gamma/epsilon?

Part of me says no because they are separate regression equations. However, at the same time, a model with the same covariate in both psi and gamma/epsilon seems funny to me.

For example, let's say you have a (static) site-covariate "A" and a dynamic site-covariate "B". Let's also say "A" and "B" are highly correlated. Now for a model with psi(A), gamma(B), epsilon(B), one might get the following result:
psi is positively associated with "A"
gamma is positively associated with "B"
epsilon is negatively associated with "B"
That doesn't seem right to me. I interpret this as meaning "A" is really important and "B" shows up because of the correlation. Or vice-versa of course.

messages.body_plain:
Hello-

I have a conceptual question regarding how to account for detection probability with single-catch systems. I am a graduate student who is new to using R, so please forgive any misuse of terminology and the elementary nature of my question.

I conducted a small mammal trapping survey using a transect design. Each sampling station along my transects had either 2 or 3 small mammal traps (Sherman or snap traps). I checked each trap station for 5 consecutive days, and I conducted 2 trapping periods. Toward the middle of my study, I switched to using only snap traps due to logistical purposes, so my project mostly involved removal sampling.

My question is, if each trap station was limited to capturing a maximum of 2 animals per station per sampling night, how should I approach accounting for detection probability? My understanding of removal sampling is that detection probability decreases with each visit because a relatively large portion of individuals are removed from the population. Unlike pitfall traps, which could theoretically “remove” a large portion of individuals, single-catch systems would limit detectability. Perhaps on a related note, due to the differences in trap number per station across my study, I will likely examine site occupancy rather than estimate true abundance.

Has anyone run into a similar question before or would have any advice on how to approach modeling detection probability?

I apologize if this post is confusing or doesn’t provide enough useful information. Please let me know if I can provide any more details for anyone who may have advice to offer.

Thank you in advance!

Erin

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

I'm not sure parameter estimation is an issue: these are regressions for z_1 being 0 or 1, and the probabilities of transitioning from occupied to unoccupied and vice versa. A very small value of what has been called P* (a cumulative probability of detecting a present organism at least during one sampling interval) poses problems, but not problems unique to having a shared covariate for each parameter. If you are using some great covariate C that more or less encapsulates the niche, and you start a study with a species being more or less in equilibrium with the environment, and there's no dispersal limitation or anything like that, then a model where C is positively associated with psi and gamma and negatively associated with epsilon could be be completely reasonable. Strong support for modeling psi and dynamics with different predictors can be an indication that the psi predictors are not great habitat descriptors.

Re. your A and B description above, A might be really important and B might be a free-rider, and if so, psi~A, gam~A, eps~A should provide better fit than psi~A, gam~B, eps~B. The predictors for gamma and epsilon don't have to be dynamic.

John

I think the main issue for the backtransformations looking odd is that you need to include the intercept always in all backtransformations when you want a prediction.

If you want the relative effect of changing a covariate by 1 unit (or some meaningful number of units) while keeping the other covariates constant, then that is another story.  Also, I would imagine that using "1 standardized unit" will usually make no sense as that depends on the the variability of the covariate in your data.  For example you'd probably want to plug in the associated standardized value for 1 year rather than the value 1.0.

The detection estimate of 5.8% is for a single visit.  For 3 visits the detection probability would be 1 - (1-0.05825069)^3 = 0.1647703.  The estimate of abundance at the average of the covariates is lambda_int = 23.26807342 but the maximum count for any one visit is 6 and most of the time it is 2 or less.  So does 5.8% still seem low?

Jim

hi Erin,

 I don't think there is a good answer to your question.  Certainly the use of both live-catch and snap traps is important and should be considered differently in the analysis.  The snap traps would preclude the use of occupancy models I think because the system is definitely not closed.  That said, some kind of modified occupancy model could be cooked up to allow for this removal process [I don't know of any references].

It might be possible to estimate density using some highly modified and novel form of spatial capture-recapture models but I think that is a long road to go down from where you're at.

 In short, I think figuring out the right analysis framework for this scenario is itself a research problem which requires some attention.

 regards,
andy

Dear all,
 I have a large occupancy data set, 6144 sites and 5 replicates.  When I run the models through occu() in unmarked they simply fail. The estimates never deviate much from the starting values. I tried alternative algorithms in optim() and they all fail too.  On the other hand the models seem to fit well using nlm() with my own likelihood function.  I'm curious if anyone has seen this before and/or if anyone has ideas for how to resolve this... I show some evidence of things below.
Thanks a lot for any ideas!
andy

(1) Here is a simply glm using the covariate Freq and Freq^2:

summary( glm(y~Freq+I(Freq^2), data.frame(data), family="binomial")  )

glm(formula = y ~ Freq + I(Freq^2), family = "binomial", data = data.frame(data))

Deviance Residuals:

-0.7656  -0.4897  -0.1112  -0.0014   4.0468

(Intercept) -4.38099    0.09960  -43.98   <2e-16 ***
Freq        -4.16516    0.13510  -30.83   <2e-16 ***
I(Freq^2)   -1.31280    0.04306  -30.48   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1

These results are correct. There is a very strong quadratic response of Freq.

(2)  Here is the occu() result:

>
>  occu(~Freq + I(Freq^2) ~1, umf , method="Nelder-Mead", start  = c( 0.3, -3.7, -4.13, -1.28 ) )

+
+

+
+
